The single most important date to watch: Friday, August 7, 8:30am ET — the July employment report.

energy: WTI crude trades near $77.81, down about 3.2% on the session, while Brent sits near $79.26, down 0.1%, as the U.S., Iran, and Oman near a 60-day interim deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz without tolls. The EIA's most recent weekly report (week ended July 31, 2026) showed commercial crude inventories rising 2.5 million barrels to 407.0 million, about 6% below the five-year seasonal average even as the Strategic Petroleum Reserve drew down 2.8 million barrels. A durable Hormuz agreement remains the key swing factor for prices into next week.
vix_and_dollar: The VIX closed near 15.81 on August 5, in the calm-to-normal range and down roughly 6% from the prior session, while the DXY sits near 99.84, essentially flat but drifting lower. The combination — falling volatility and a soft dollar — points to continued risk appetite as long as the Hormuz de-escalation holds.
mortgage_rate: The 30-year fixed mortgage averaged 6.66% in Freddie Mac's July 30, 2026 survey, up from 6.58% the week prior. Rates near multi-week highs are working against the affordability gains housing had clawed back earlier this year, even as wage growth continues to outpace home-price growth nationally.
personal_finance_deep_dive: Total U.S. household debt reached a record $18.79 trillion in the first quarter, per the New York Fed, but the composition matters more than the headline number: credit card balances actually fell $25 billion quarter-over-quarter to $1.25 trillion, the normal seasonal pattern after Q4 spending, yet remain 5.9% higher than a year ago. Mortgage, auto, and HELOC balances all grew, signaling households are still willing to take on debt for big-ticket items even as revolving balances stay historically elevated. The pattern suggests financial stress is concentrated in the households already carrying card balances rather than broadening across the population.
wealth_building_deep_dive: Vanguard's 25th annual How America Saves report found 71% of 401(k) plans now include automatic escalation, up sharply from prior years, and 31% of participants had their deferral rate bumped up automatically in 2025 alone. The mechanism works because it converts a decision — asking an employee to actively choose more savings — into a default that only requires opting out, and most people never do. A practical takeaway: anyone whose plan offers auto-escalation but hasn't turned it on can typically enable a 1%-per-year increase in a few clicks through their plan's website, capturing the same effect without waiting for a raise.
